title: Thyroid storm
summary: A life-threatening emergency. The order of the first drugs matters.

mnemonic.cue: Stop the factory → shut the gates → calm the body
expansion: Gates: iodide blocks release, at least 1 hour after the thionamide

root.content: High fever, tachycardia, delirium in a thyrotoxic patient

node.content: Decompensation lasts about 72 h on average

cards.text: Find and treat the trigger (e.g., infection)

cards.trapReason: Iodide given first could provide substrate to make even more thyroid hormone. Give it at least 1 hour after the thionamide.
Aspirin and other NSAIDs may displace bound thyroid hormone. Use acetaminophen for fever.
RAI treatment is itself a precipitating factor for thyroid storm, not an emergency treatment.

s-synth.explanation: ATDs block new hormone synthesis. Large-dose PTU may be preferred because it also blocks peripheral T4 → T3 conversion; methimazole lasts longer. Tablets can go by gastric or rectal tube.

s-release.explanation: Iodides rapidly block release of preformed hormone. Give them at least 1 hour after the thionamide so the gland can't use the iodide.

s-adrenergic.explanation: β-Blockers inhibit the effects of severe thyrotoxicosis. Esmolol is preferred in the ICU: usable with lung disease or heart-failure risk and rapidly reversible.

s-steroid.explanation: Corticosteroids are generally recommended; the benefit may come from their antipyretic effect and BP stabilization.

s-antipyretic.explanation: Acetaminophen is the antipyretic. Avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs, which may displace bound thyroid hormone.

s-trigger.explanation: Treat what precipitated the storm: infection, trauma, surgery, RAI treatment, or ATD withdrawal.

s-refractory.explanation: Plasmapheresis and peritoneal dialysis have been used to remove excess hormone when conservative measures fail, although they don't always work.
